props.title: September Sessions
props.initialSlug: Jack Johnson surfs & jams in Indonesia

sections.content: September Sessions represents a pivotal moment in surf documentary filmmaking, shot by Jack Johnson before his music career exploded. The film captures an intimate portrait of professional surfers in Indonesia immediately following 9/11, when travel fears kept most tourists away. It shares DNA with earlier groundbreaking surf docs like The Endless Summer (1966) and Morning of the Earth (1971), but strips away the polished narration for a raw, vérité approach. Johnson's cinematography in the water creates an immersive experience that influenced later surf films like View From a Blue Moon (2015).

sections.content: The film's soundtrack, featuring Jack Johnson's own music alongside G. Love and other artists, established a new template for surf film scoring. Previous surf documentaries relied heavily on rock and psychedelic music, but September Sessions brought in acoustic folk and laid-back Hawaiian sounds that perfectly matched its intimate portrayal of wave riding. This musical approach influenced countless surf films that followed, including A Brokedown Melody (2004) and Thicker Than Water (2000).

What sets September Sessions apart is its capturing of a specific moment in surfing history. Post-9/11 fear created eerily empty Indonesian lineups, allowing the film's subjects - including Kelly Slater and Rob Machado - to surf perfect waves without crowds. This accidental timing created a time capsule of professional surfing at a crossroads between the competitive circuit and the emerging "soul surfing" movement championed by films like Single Fin: Yellow (2003). SUBHEAD: Impact on Modern Surf Cinema

movies.title: The Present
movies.slug: A meditative look at modern surf culture featuring Dave Rastovich

sections.content: Johnson's naturalistic filming style in September Sessions helped establish a new aesthetic in surf documentaries that continues today. Films like Distance Between Dreams (2016) and Let's Be Frank (2016) follow this intimate, character-driven approach rather than the bombastic style of earlier surf films. The focus stays on the relationship between surfer and wave, with minimal interference from flashy editing or heavy narration.
